slides.title: Attributes of actors
points: Actor attributes help you compare threat actors by where they operate, the resources available to them, and their technical sophistication.
Security+ Objective 2.1: compare and contrast common threat actors and motivations.

slides.title: Internal / External
slides.teach: Describes whether the actor originates from inside the organization or outside it.

course.learn: Describes whether the actor originates from inside the organization or outside it.

breakdown.explanation: Ask where the actor starts relative to the organization.
Employee with access, External attacker on the internet

course.why: Location and trust position affect the defenses, visibility, and access paths available to the attacker.
course.example: A database administrator misuses valid credentials from inside the organization.
course.exam: Inside the company → INTERNAL; outside the organization → EXTERNAL.
course.check_q: What attribute distinguishes an employee from an internet-based attacker?

slides.title: Resources / Funding
slides.teach: Describes how much money, infrastructure, time, staffing, and tooling an actor can use.

course.learn: Describes how much money, infrastructure, time, staffing, and tooling an actor can use.

breakdown.explanation: Ask how much support the actor has available.
Government funding, Criminal infrastructure, Minimal personal resources

course.why: Greater resources can enable persistence, custom tooling, large infrastructure, and longer campaigns.
course.example: A state-backed group maintains multiple command-and-control networks and dedicated research teams.
course.check_q: Which attribute describes the money and infrastructure available to an actor?

slides.title: Level of Sophistication / Capability
slides.teach: Describes the actor’s technical skill, operational maturity, tooling, and ability to conduct complex attacks.

course.learn: Describes the actor’s technical skill, operational maturity, tooling, and ability to conduct complex attacks.

breakdown.explanation: Ask how advanced the actor is.
Custom malware, Zero-day capability, Basic public scripts

course.why: Capability affects the complexity, stealth, persistence, and technical difficulty of the attacks an actor can perform.
course.example: An attacker develops custom malware, exploits an unknown vulnerability, and remains undetected for months.
course.exam: Custom tools + stealth + long campaign → HIGH SOPHISTICATION.
course.check_q: Which attribute describes how technically advanced an actor is?

hero.title: Attributes of actors
hero.intro: Actor attributes help you compare threat actors by where they operate, the resources available to them, and their technical sophistication.

blocks.title: Attributes of actors
blocks.prompt: Compare the clues in the scenario and identify the most likely actor, attribute, or motivation.

cards.name: Internal / External
cards.definition: Describes whether the actor originates from inside the organization or outside it.

cards.name: Resources / Funding
cards.definition: Describes how much money, infrastructure, time, staffing, and tooling an actor can use.

cards.name: Level of Sophistication / Capability
cards.definition: Describes the actor’s technical skill, operational maturity, tooling, and ability to conduct complex attacks.

blocks.title: Where are they, how much support, and how capable?
items: Internal actors already have some degree of organizational access or trust.
Example: A database administrator misuses legitimate credentials.
External actors begin outside the trusted organization.
Example: A criminal group attacks an internet-facing VPN.
Funding affects persistence, tooling, staffing, and operational scale.
Example: A state-backed team maintains multiple command-and-control infrastructures.
Custom tools + stealth + long campaign → HIGH SOPHISTICATION
Advanced actors can build custom tools and sustain complex operations.
Example: An actor develops custom malware and evades detection for months.
Public scripts + obvious mistakes → LOW SOPHISTICATION
Less-capable actors often rely on existing tools and make noisy mistakes.
Example: An attacker runs a common script without modifying it.
blocks.example: Memory: Internal/external = WHERE · Resources = SUPPORT · Sophistication = CAPABILITY.

questions.q: A database administrator misuses valid credentials to steal data. Which actor attribute is most directly highlighted?
questions.explanation: The administrator originates inside the organization and already has legitimate access.

questions.q: A criminal group attacks an internet-facing VPN from infrastructure outside the company. Which attribute best describes its position?
questions.explanation: The actor begins outside the organization.

questions.q: A state-backed team maintains global infrastructure, dedicated staff, and expensive research capabilities. Which attribute is most clearly demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Large infrastructure and dedicated staffing indicate substantial resources and funding.

questions.q: An attacker develops custom malware, exploits a previously unknown flaw, and remains undetected for months. Which attribute is most evident?
questions.explanation: Custom malware, advanced exploitation, and stealth indicate high sophistication.

questions.q: An attacker uses a common public script without modification and makes obvious operational mistakes. Which attribute is most likely?
questions.explanation: Reliance on unmodified public tools and obvious mistakes indicates lower sophistication.

questions.q: Which actor attribute asks how much money, infrastructure, time, and staffing are available?
questions.explanation: Resources/funding describes the support available to an actor.
